In the following snippet

import Mathlib

def f {C : ℕ} (x : Fin C) : Fin (C + 1) := x.castSucc
def g {D : ℕ} (x : Fin D) : ℕ := x.val

/-- Transporting a `Fin` along an equality of bounds preserves the underlying value. -/
private lemma fin_val_eq_of_heq {n m : ℕ} (h : n = m) (i : Fin n) :
    (h ▸ i).val = i.val := by subst h; rfl

theorem s (x: List ℕ) (i : Fin x.length) :
  let S := {s : List ℕ // s.length = x.length}
  let x₀ : S := ⟨List.replicate x.length 0, by simp_all only [List.length_replicate]⟩
  g (f (x₀.property ▸ i)) = g (f i) := by
    intro S x₀
    simp only [g, f, Fin.val_castSucc]
    let p := x₀.property

    -- exact fin_val_eq_of_heq p.symm i

    -- simplifying the .val projection away does not simplify the goal
    -- unfold x₀ at p ⊢
    -- simp only at p ⊢

    rw [p]

the rewrite would fail that the motive used by Eq.rec does not type check. Is the reason for this the Subtype.val projection or could the type casting affect this? Because then trying to simplify it away (last commented block) doesn't simplify the goal accordingly. So far the only way to make this work is to use subst with a simpler lemma (first commented block).
This topic was moved here from #lean4 > Eq.rec chokes doesn't type check with type cast by Plamen Dimitrov.
It doesn't directly answer your question, but judging by your snippet you may be looking for the functionality that docs#Fin.cast provides

In this case I would have tried even Fin.val_cast but it doesn't play well with the ▸ casting:

exact Fin.val_cast p.symm i

Type mismatch
  Fin.val_cast (Eq.symm p) i
has type
  ↑(Fin.cast ⋯ i) = ↑i
but is expected to have type
  ↑(⋯ ▸ i) = ↑i

as in Lean it seems the Fin.cast is not definitionally equal to (⋯ ▸ i).
Indeed. My point is that one should avoid using the Eq.rec notation and use the preexisting API that exists for Fin.cast.

Indeed, Fin.cast_eq_cast could brings us a bit closer like:

import Mathlib

def f {C : ℕ} (x : Fin C) : Fin (C + 1) := x.castSucc
def g {D : ℕ} (x : Fin D) : ℕ := x.val

theorem s (x: List ℕ) (i : Fin x.length) :
  let S := {s : List ℕ // s.length = x.length}
  let x₀ : S := ⟨List.replicate x.length 0, by simp_all only [List.length_replicate]⟩
  g (f (x₀.property ▸ i)) = g (f i) := by
    intro S x₀
    simp only [g, f, Fin.val_castSucc]
    let p := x₀.property

    -- rw [p]
    have := Fin.val_cast p.symm i
    rw [Fin.cast_eq_cast] at this
    exact this

but still ends with

Type mismatch
  this
has type
  ↑(cast ⋯ i) = ↑i
but is expected to have type
  ↑(⋯ ▸ i) = ↑i

which now seems to make more sense considering ▸ is a macro built on top of Eq.rec. Two follow-ups:
1) It seems that indeed we should not use the macro in theorems and rely on cast and in this case even better Fin.cast. What is suggested most appropriate use for the macro then?
2) This begs the question why do we have three different ways to achieve the same cast here instead of a single centralized approach? I think it will be implicitly assumed by many users that these should do the same but instead they either require additional theorems or worse yet have none. In short, what is the importance of differentiating these approaches?
the benefit of having Fin.cast separately is that docs#Fin.val_cast is a definitional equality

When I needed to spend significant time on dealing with casting, I often found it easier to switch to bare Nat and pass additional hypotheses when necessary.

This might be oversimplification, but the example can be proven by just rfl:

def f {C : Nat} (x : Nat) (_h : x < C) : Nat := x
def g {D : Nat} (x : Nat) (_h : x < D) : Nat := x

theorem s (x: List Nat) (i : Nat) (h : i < x.length) :
    g (D := x.length + 1) (f i h) (by grind [f]) = g (D := x.length + 1) (f i h) (by grind [f]) := by
  rfl

Here's how you're supposed to do this with Fin.cast:

import Mathlib

def f {C : ℕ} (x : Fin C) : Fin (C + 1) := x.castSucc
def g {D : ℕ} (x : Fin D) : ℕ := x.val

theorem s (x: List ℕ) (i : Fin x.length) :
  let S := {s : List ℕ // s.length = x.length}
  let x₀ : S := ⟨List.replicate x.length 0, by simp_all only [List.length_replicate]⟩
  g (f (i.cast x₀.property.symm)) = g (f i) := rfl

A reply to the original post: one can use rw! instead of rw as it also rewrites in the types of terms (I'm not an expert on how rw! works but, but this is my understanding).

import Mathlib

def f {C : ℕ} (x : Fin C) : Fin (C + 1) := x.castSucc
def g {D : ℕ} (x : Fin D) : ℕ := x.val

/-- Transporting a `Fin` along an equality of bounds preserves the underlying value. -/
private lemma fin_val_eq_of_heq {n m : ℕ} (h : n = m) (i : Fin n) :
    (h ▸ i).val = i.val := by subst h; rfl

theorem s (x: List ℕ) (i : Fin x.length) :
  let S := {s : List ℕ // s.length = x.length}
  let x₀ : S := ⟨List.replicate x.length 0, by simp_all only [List.length_replicate]⟩
  g (f (x₀.property ▸ i)) = g (f i) := by
    intro S x₀
    simp only [g, f, Fin.val_castSucc]
    let p := x₀.property
    rw! [p]
    rfl

I guess it is a way to make things work or rebuild from the ground up in some sense but it avoids the type theory advantage of bundling the properties in the type. Let's say that my point is not as much about solving this as to why there are incompatible operators like the ▸ cast when others are meant to be used and offer advantages over it.

Fin.cast itself is implemented using ▸ under the hood. In that sense, ▸ is the primitive operation, while Fin.cast provides more specialized APIs together with useful lemmas.

Let's say that my point is not as much about solving this as to why there are incompatible operators like the ▸ cast when others are meant to be used and offer advantages over it.

My point was that dependent types come with the trade-off that one sometimes has to spend time on these (non-essential) casts. Avoiding dependent types can therefore be a perfectly valid design choice in such situations.

Fin.cast itself is implemented using ▸ under the hood. In that sense, ▸ is the primitive operation, while Fin.cast provides more specialized APIs together with useful lemmas.

I see, this makes sense. However, then shouldn't some of the casting lemmas needed above also be valid for the more primitive ▸ cast? Because of if such a cast is more general in nature there could still be properties it retains on its own level of generality. I guess this could be quite a technical difference somewhere but at least on a more theoretical and distant point of view I would have thought that even as a weaker definition ▸ should have some properties shared with Fin.cast and at least some of the separation of lemmas seems artificial and purely technical.

My point was that dependent types come with the trade-off that one sometimes has to spend time on these (non-essential) casts. Avoiding dependent types can therefore be a perfectly valid design choice in such situations.

Exactly, and decomposing complex types into simpler types and their properties either fully decoupled or bundled in "small enough" subtypes is also part of this that seems closer to classical math and further away from type theory yet brings to a lot of low hanging fruits much faster.

I mean theorems imitating the ones above but applying to the triangle cast macro like

theorem triangle_val_cast {n m : ℕ} (h : n = m) (i : Fin n) : (h ▸ i).val = i.val := by
  subst h
  simp_all only

theorem triangle_cast_eq_cast {n m : ℕ} (h : n = m) (i : Fin n) : h ▸ i = cast (by subst h ; simp_all only) i := by
  subst h
  simp_all only [cast_eq]
